summary: Adds a new 78-line markdown resource arguing that a good adversarial review of an AI chatbot depends on discipline: explicit impact-first threat model, diverse and partly independent testers, taxonomy-anchored reproducible methodology, manual plus automated probing, severity grading, and a closed remediate-retest loop. It cites NIST, OWASP, MITRE ATLAS, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepMind, and Feffer et al., lists pitfalls of weak reviews, gives a four-stage recommendation, and closes with caveats about field immaturity and metric fragility.

claims.text: Feffer et al. (AIES 2024) found red-teaming purposes often vague and warned unstructured red teaming verges on security theater.
NIST AI 600-1 defines 12 GenAI risk categories and places red teaming under Measure as a recurring activity.
OpenAI white paper arXiv 2503.16431 lays out four campaign design steps and cohort diversity axes.
Crescendomation achieves 29-61% higher performance on GPT-4 and 49-71% on Gemini-Pro, 98% binary success on GPT-4.
Constitutional Classifiers cut jailbreak success from 86% to 4.4% at 23.7% compute overhead and 0.38% refusal rise.
Constitutional Classifiers++ released January 9, 2026 at ~1% additional compute with no universal jailbreak found.

risks.note: Bug-bounty figures (405 of ~800, 339 participants, 300,000 interactions, 8 levels) have no source link.
'One 2026 methodological paper warns' about ASR validity is unnamed and uncited.
'Most processes remain limited to English' attributed to no source.
OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications dated 2026 with no citation; line 72 calls it 'ASI Top 10'.

least_confident: I could not check the many specific numbers and dates (Crescendo percentages, Constitutional Classifiers stats, the January 9, 2026 release) against their primary sources.
